question: The events in Poland have shocked us all. The President of the Constitutional Tribunal was suspended by someone whose legitimacy as a judge is in dispute1, and who has never even taken an oath before the country’s head of state2. The police were deployed against protesters and, according to reports, tried to prevent the Tribunal’s leadership, and even the Polish President himself, from entering the building3.
Given how in the past the Commission has trumpeted its firm stance on judicial independence, one might have expected it to issue a sharp response.

But instead of condemning these acts of political and police coercion, it merely reiterated that the power to elect judges lies with the Sejm, and issued a general call to respect the constitution – all of which gives the impression that the Commission condones, at the very least, the police’s intervention. Neither is this the first time the Commission has shown such ‘restraint’.

It went equally quiet when opposition figures in Slovakia were being prosecuted and placed in detention between 2020 and 2022, and when the Romanian presidential elections were annulled. After the elections in Hungary, too, it turned a blind eye to the kinds of constitutional and personnel changes that in the past it would not have hesitated to respond to or describe as threats to the rule of law. 1.

What specific criteria does the Commission use to assess interference in the independence of judges and, when applying such criteria, how does it ensure it is not swayed by the political orientation of the government in the Member State concerned?

Why, during the recent events in Poland, did it not condemn the police for putting pressure on the Constitutional Tribunal and trying to prevent officials, including the Polish President, from entering the building, even though in other cases it has labelled much more minor interventions as threats to the rule of law?
